Project: React. Upgrade being assessed: 17 -> 18.
This change was introduced in release 18. Source: How to Upgrade to React 18 (official_migration_guide). Section: Automatic Batching.
Version facts from package metadata for this release (authoritative for version numbers): none

ITEM:
<<<
React 18 adds out-of-the-box performance improvements by doing more batching by default. Batching is when React groups multiple state updates into a single re-render for better performance. Before React 18, we only batched updates inside React event handlers. Updates inside of promises, setTimeout, native event handlers, or any other event were not batched in React by default: // Before React 18 only React events were batched function handleClick() { setCount(c => c + 1); setFlag(f => !f); // React will only re-render once at the end (that's batching!) } setTimeout(() => { setCount(c => c + 1); setFlag(f => !f); // React will render twice, once for each state update (no batching) }, 1000);
>>>

PARENT CONTEXT (same section, for disambiguation only):
<<<
Automatic Batching: React 18 adds out-of-the-box performance improvements by doing more batching by default. Batching is when React groups multiple state updates into a single re-render for better performance. Before React 18, we only batched updates inside React event handlers. Updates inside of promises, setTimeout, native event handlers, or any other event were not batched in React by default: // Before React 18 only React events were batched function handleClick() { setCount(c => c + 1); setFlag(f => !f); // React will only re-render once at the end (that's batching!) } setTimeout(() => { setCount(c => c + 1); setFlag(f => !f); // React will render twice, once for each state update (no batching) }, 1000); Starting in React 18 with createRoot, all updates will be automatically batched, no matter where they originate from. This means that updates inside of timeouts, promises, native event handlers or any other event will batch the same way as updates inside of React events: // After React 18 updates inside of timeouts, promises, // native event handlers or any other event are batched. function handleClick() { setCount(c => c + 1); setFlag(f => !f); // React will only re-render once at the end (that's batching!) } setTimeout(() => { setCount(c => c + 1); setFlag(f => !f); // React will only re-render once at the end (that's batching!) }, 1000); This is a breaking change, but we expect this to result in less work rendering, and therefore better performance in your applications. To opt-out of automatic batching, you can use flushSync: import { flushSync } from 'react-dom'; function handleClick() { flushSync(() => { setCounter(c => c + 1); }); // React has updated the DOM by now flushSync(() => { setFlag(f => !f); }); // React has updated the DOM by now } For more information, see the Automatic batching deep dive.
>>>

Decide the disposition:
- "risk": the item describes something that can break an app/deployment, require migration work, or create operational risk.
- "context": it is accurate but needs no action at 18 (no user action required, deprecated-but-working, additive feature). Give the reason.

For "risk", produce one or more risk paths. Use separate paths for separate symbols/APIs when they can be checked independently. Hard rules:
1. Every condition has at least one quote copied EXACTLY, character for character, from ITEM or PARENT CONTEXT (contiguous span, 3-40 words, no ellipses, no added words). Do not fix typos or formatting.
2. Each path has exactly one condition with category "version" stating that the upgrade crosses release 18 (quote the text that ties the change to this release, or the change statement itself), and at least one application/deployment condition (category api_usage, configuration, dependency, runtime, deployment, database, behavior or test_coverage) describing what the app or deployment must use/have for the risk to apply.
3. If the text does not state something you need, do not assert it: use role "uncertain" and explain in ambiguities. Use derived_by "inference" for any condition not directly stated.
4. role: "required" (must hold), "alternative" (any one of the alternatives suffices), "optional" (raises impact), "disqualifying" (if it holds, the risk does NOT apply, e.g. not using the new opt-in API), "uncertain".
5. operator/expected_value must be checkable: e.g. operator "present" with expected_value the literal symbol; "less_than" with a version; "equals" with a setting value. expected_value is a string.
6. If a replacement API/setting/version is named, put the migration step in suggested_actions and add a condition for any behavior that differs in the replacement when the text states one.
7. search_queries: for app-side conditions with a literal symbol, give ripgrep regexes (tool "ripgrep"), kubectl commands (tool "kubectl") or SQL (tool "sql") that would find usage. Empty list if no literal symbol.
8. primary_symbol: the most specific identifier of the change (full apiVersion string like "policy/v1beta1", setting name, function, flag, or runtime name like "Python"/"Node.js"). symbols: all identifiers involved.
9. risk_level rubric: critical = upgrade fails or data is at risk for most users meeting the conditions (e.g. unsupported runtime/database version, removed API version that stops serving); high = code or config meeting the conditions breaks at upgrade; medium = behavior change or migration with a clear workaround; low = edge case, cosmetic, or warning-only.
10. fires_at: "upgrade" (at upgrade time), "first_use" (when a feature is first exercised), "rotation" (on credential/password rotation), "rollout" (on deployment rollout), "future_removal" (deprecated now, removed later).
11. applies_to: fill upgrade_method (e.g. "pg_upgrade", "dump/restore"), cluster_type, or from_versions (a version specifier like "<3.1") ONLY if the text restricts applicability; otherwise null.
Do not output confidence.

paths.path_name: Automatic batching changes render timing for state updates outside React event handlers
paths.description: Before React 18, state updates inside promises, setTimeout, native event handlers, or other non-React events were not batched and each caused a re-render. With createRoot in React 18, all updates are batched into a single re-render regardless of origin. The guide labels this a breaking change. Code that relied on a synchronous re-render or DOM update between consecutive state updates in those contexts may behave differently. The workaround is flushSync.

conditions.statement: The upgrade crosses React 18, where automatic batching of all updates is introduced
quotes: React 18 adds out-of-the-box performance improvements by doing more batching by default.
conditions.relevance: Ties the batching change to release 18.

conditions.statement: The application renders with createRoot, since the guide says the new batching applies starting in React 18 with createRoot
quotes: Starting in React 18 with createRoot, all updates will be automatically batched, no matter where they originate from.
conditions.relevance: Automatic batching for all update sources is stated to apply with createRoot.
ambiguities: The text does not say what batching behavior applies if the app keeps the legacy ReactDOM.render root.

conditions.statement: State updates (e.g., setState or hook setters) are made inside promises, setTimeout, native event handlers, or other non-React events
conditions.expected_value: state updates inside setTimeout, promises, or native event handlers
quotes: Updates inside of promises, setTimeout, native event handlers, or any other event were not batched in React by default
conditions.relevance: These updates previously rendered once each and will now be batched into one re-render.
ambiguities: The text does not state which specific code patterns break, only that render behavior changes.

conditions.statement: Code depends on a re-render or DOM update occurring between consecutive state updates outside React event handlers
conditions.expected_value: reliance on a separate render per state update
quotes: React will render twice, once for each state update (no batching)
conditions.relevance: Such code observes different render timing after the change; the guide states updates now batch into one render.
ambiguities: The text does not explicitly say that application code relies on per-update renders; this is inferred from calling the change breaking.

conditions.statement: The application already uses flushSync to opt out of batching for the affected updates, in which case the batching change does not alter them
quotes: To opt-out of automatic batching, you can use flushSync:
conditions.relevance: Updates wrapped in flushSync are flushed immediately, so they retain unbatched behavior.
ambiguities: Disqualifies only the updates wrapped in flushSync, not the whole application.

suggested_actions: Audit state updates inside setTimeout, promises, and native event handlers for reliance on one render per update.
Wrap updates that must be rendered synchronously in flushSync imported from 'react-dom' to opt out of automatic batching.
Test affected components after migrating to createRoot.
